core_idea: The phrase 'Word of the Lord' in Scripture refers not to the Bible but to a divine person, Jesus Christ, who is both identified with Yahweh and distinguished from Him, acting as the mediator of creation, revelation, and salvation throughout the Old Testament and ultimately incarnate in the Gospel of John.

segments.reason: Introduces the key point that 'word of God' in the Bible never refers to the Bible itself, but to a person; establishes the problem of modern misinterpretation.
Explains the Hebrew term 'debar Yahweh' and its broad meaning (word, matter, thing), showing it can be read as 'the Yahweh word'—a personal figure like the angel of the Lord.
Uses Philo of Alexandria as a case study to show that the logos was understood within Second Temple Judaism as a personal mediator, not a Greek philosophical concept.
Discusses the Targums, which insert 'Memra' (word) where Yahweh appears bodily, showing that Jewish interpreters saw the Word as a distinct divine person who can be seen.
Exegesis of Genesis 15: the Word of the Lord appears to Abram, is called Yahweh by Abram, and does not correct him—demonstrating the Word is both Yahweh and distinct.
Exegesis of 1 Samuel 3: the Word of the Lord appears visually to Samuel, and knowing God is equated with seeing the Word; establishes the Word as the means of knowing Yahweh.
Exegesis of Jeremiah 1: the Word of the Lord comes to Jeremiah, speaks as Yahweh, and physically touches his mouth—reinforcing the Word as a personal, divine agent.
Summarizes three key points: the Word is a person, seen and interacted with bodily, and is both Yahweh and distinguished from Yahweh—a second divine person.
Begins exegesis of John 1:1, showing that 'in the beginning was the Word' uses the imperfect tense, meaning the Word already existed before creation—identifying Christ as the pre-existent Word.
Continues John 1:1-2: the Word was 'with God' (co-located, distinct) and 'was God' (identified)—the same pattern as the Old Testament Word of the Lord.
Exegesis of John 1:3: all things came into being through the Word, and he is not in the category of created things—affirming his role as Creator and his uncreated nature.
Exegesis of John 1:4-5: the light is the life of Christ, identified with the light of Genesis 1, and its purpose is to bring salvation (theosis) to humanity from the very beginning.

Exegesis of John 1:10-13: the Word was in the world (creation), came to his own people (Israel), and was rejected; yet those who received him became children of God—showing the Word's work in the Old Testament.
Exegesis of John 1:14: the Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' among us, identifying Jesus as the same Word who appeared throughout the Old Testament, now incarnate.
Exegesis of John 1:18: no one has seen the Father, but the unique God (the Word) has made Him known—tying the entire Old Testament revelation of the Word to Christ.
Summarizes the Word as Christ in his revelatory role: the interface between God and creation, the agent of creation, and the source of salvation/light from the beginning.
Applies the teaching: because Christ is the logos (order, meaning) behind all creation, all true knowledge leads to Him, and compartmentalizing faith from life is false.
